## Before class you read

**Shukla**, *Credit Scoring of Thin File Consumers*.

::: {.muted}
Harvard Dataverse, DOI 10.7910/DVN/EGAIKO · CC BY 4.0 · includes Python code
:::

A "thin file" consumer has almost no credit history. The paper is about
classifying people **the data barely describes** — which is exactly the
situation where the threshold matters more than the model.

::: {.check}
This is one of the sessions where you work with the **authors' own data**, not
a synthetic stand-in.
:::

## Today's question

> *Which European countries will fall into the bottom decile of productivity
> growth **next year**?*

::: {.tight}
- The outcome is binary
- It is **rare** — about one country in ten
- Getting it wrong in one direction costs more than the other
:::

# Why not least squares {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The linear probability model

You *can* regress a 0/1 outcome on $X$ by OLS. Economists do it often, and it
has real virtues — the coefficients are marginal effects, and it is robust.

But:

::: {.tight}
- Fitted values go **below 0 and above 1**, which are not probabilities
- The errors are heteroskedastic by construction
- The fit is pulled around by points far from the boundary
:::

::: {.muted}
The LPM is defensible for an average effect. It is a poor basis for a *decision*.
:::

## Model the log-odds instead

$$\log\frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = x'\beta \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad p(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x'\beta}}$$

::: {.check}
The logistic function maps the whole real line into $(0,1)$. No fitted value can
ever be an impossible probability.
:::

## What the coefficients mean

$\beta_j$ is the change in **log-odds** for a one-unit change in $x_j$.

::: {.tight}
- $e^{\beta_j}$ is the **odds ratio** — multiplicative, not additive
- The effect on the *probability* depends on where you are on the curve
- Near $p = 0.5$ the curve is steepest; in the tails it is nearly flat
:::

::: {.warn}
"A one-point rise in the barrier index raises the probability by $\beta$" is
wrong. There is no single such number. Report the odds ratio, or a marginal
effect evaluated at a stated point.
:::

## Fitting it

There is no closed form. We maximise the log-likelihood

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \Big[ y_i \, x_i'\beta - \log\big(1 + e^{x_i'\beta}\big) \Big]$$

which is **concave**, so the maximum is unique and the optimiser converges.

::: {.muted}
Concavity is why logistic regression is boring to fit and trees are not.
:::

## Separation

If some predictor perfectly splits the classes, the likelihood is maximised by
sending $\beta \to \infty$.

::: {.tight}
- Coefficients explode; standard errors explode faster
- Software may report "convergence" anyway
- It is *more* common in small samples — like a 30-country panel
:::

::: {.check}
A penalty fixes it. Which is the next section.
:::

# Penalised logistic {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The same two penalties

$$\min_\beta \; -\ell(\beta) + \lambda\left(\alpha\|\beta\|_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\right)$$

Everything from Session 05 carries over:

::: {.tight}
- $\ell_2$ shrinks and shares; $\ell_1$ selects
- Standardise first, inside the pipeline
- Choose $\lambda$ by cross-validation, grouped by country
:::

::: {.warn}
In `scikit-learn` the logistic penalty is parameterised by `C`, which is
**$1/\lambda$**. Larger `C` means *less* regularisation. This trips up everyone
once.
:::

# The data {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The label

```python
import pandas as pd

core = pd.read_parquet("data/spine/core.parquet")
print(core.falling_behind_next.mean())      # 0.100
print(core.falling_behind_next.isna().sum())  # 30
```

::: {.tight}
- The rate is **exactly 10% by construction** — the threshold is the within-year
  bottom decile
- **30 rows are NaN**: the last year of each of 30 countries
:::

## That NaN is not a defect

`falling_behind_next` is next year's outcome. For 2024 there is no next year.

::: {.check}
Dropping those 30 rows is **correct**. Imputing them would be inventing the
future — the exact error this course exists to prevent.
:::

::: {.warn}
Be equally careful the other way: if you build features from the *same* year as
the label without lagging, you have used information that would not have been
available when the prediction had to be made.
:::

## Base rate is a benchmark

A model that predicts "never falls behind" for every country is **90% accurate**.

::: {.warn}
If your model reports 91% accuracy, it has added one percentage point over
saying nothing at all. Accuracy on an imbalanced problem is not a measure of
skill — it is a measure of the base rate.
:::

# Doing it {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Set up

```python
import numpy as np

d = core.dropna(subset=["falling_behind_next"]).copy()
d = d.sort_values(["geo", "time"])

feat = ["gdp_pc_eur", "population", "employment_ths",
        "productivity_idx", "gfcf_meur", "prod_growth"]
X = d[feat].fillna(d[feat].median())
y = d["falling_behind_next"].astype(int)

print(X.shape, y.mean().round(3))     # (420, 6), 0.1
```

## Fit it

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold

clf = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegressionCV(Cs=np.logspace(-3, 3, 30), penalty="l2",
                         cv=5, scoring="neg_log_loss", max_iter=5000),
)
clf.fit(X, y)
```

::: {.check}
Scored by **log loss**, not accuracy. Log loss rewards well-calibrated
probabilities; accuracy rewards guessing the majority class.
:::

## Why the inner `cv` is just `5`

::: {.warn}
A precomputed `GroupKFold(...).split(...)` holds row positions for the
**whole** dataset. Nest it inside the outer loop on the next slide and those
positions point past the end of the training subset — an `IndexError`, if you
are lucky enough to get one.
:::

::: {.check}
The grouping belongs on the **outer** loop, which is where it protects you.
:::

## Out-of-sample probabilities

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

p = cross_val_predict(clf, X, y, cv=GroupKFold(5).split(X, y, d["geo"]),
                      method="predict_proba")[:, 1]

print("mean predicted:", p.mean().round(3), " actual:", y.mean().round(3))
```

::: {.muted}
Those two numbers should be close. If the mean predicted probability is far from
the base rate, the model is miscalibrated before you have chosen any threshold.
:::

# Judging it {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## ROC is the wrong picture here

The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR. With 90% negatives, the FPR denominator is
enormous, so a great many false positives barely move the curve.

::: {.check}
Use the **precision–recall** curve when the positive class is rare. Its baseline
is the base rate — 0.10 here — not 0.5.
:::

```python
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
print("ROC AUC :", round(roc_auc_score(y, p), 3))
print("PR  AUC :", round(average_precision_score(y, p), 3), " baseline", round(y.mean(), 3))
```

## Calibration

```python
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

frac, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins=8, strategy="quantile")
plt.plot(mean_pred, frac, "o-"); plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--")
plt.xlabel("predicted probability"); plt.ylabel("observed frequency")
```

::: {.check}
On the diagonal, "0.3" means it happens 30% of the time. That is what makes a
probability usable by somebody making a decision.
:::

# The threshold {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## 0.5 is not a default. It is a claim.

Classifying at $p > 0.5$ asserts that a false positive and a false negative cost
the same.

::: {.warn}
For "which countries need policy attention?", they obviously do not. Missing a
country that falls behind is not the same as sending an analyst to one that was
fine.
:::

## Choose it with a loss

Let $c_{FN}$ be the cost of a miss and $c_{FP}$ the cost of a false alarm. The
threshold that minimises expected cost is

$$t^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}$$

::: {.tight}
- Missing is 4× as costly → $t^\star = 0.2$
- Equal costs → $t^\star = 0.5$
:::

::: {.check}
You will not know these costs precisely. State the ratio you assumed, and show
how the answer moves when it changes.
:::

## Sweep it

```python
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score

rows = []
for t in np.arange(0.05, 0.65, 0.05):
    yhat = (p >= t).astype(int)
    rows.append((round(t, 2), yhat.sum(),
                 round(precision_score(y, yhat, zero_division=0), 3),
                 round(recall_score(y, yhat), 3)))

print(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["threshold", "flagged", "precision", "recall"]))
```

::: {.muted}
Read the "flagged" column as a workload: how many countries would you actually
have to look at?
:::

## What to report

::: {.tight}
- The **base rate**, first, so accuracy can be read against it
- PR AUC rather than ROC AUC, with the baseline stated
- A calibration plot, or a sentence about what it showed
- The **threshold you chose and the cost ratio implying it**
- Precision and recall *at that threshold* — not the maximum over all thresholds
:::

::: {.warn}
Reporting the best F1 over a swept threshold, chosen on the same data you
evaluate on, is a leak. Choose the threshold on training folds.
:::

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Reporting accuracy | 90% means nothing at a 10% base rate |
| Threshold left at 0.5 | An economic assumption made silently |
| ROC AUC on rare events | Looks strong, hides false positives |
| Imputing the 30 NaN labels | Inventing the future |
| `C` read as a penalty | Regularisation backwards |
| Same-year features | Leakage from the prediction date |
